blocks.text: Mass spectrometry can find the relative abundance of isotopes experimentally. The relative abundance is the proportion of a particular isotope in the natural mixture of isotopes; for example, chlorine is 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37. The heights of the peaks in a mass spectrum show the proportion of each isotope: for boron, B-10 has a relative abundance of 19.9% and B-11 of 80.1%.

blocks.title: Relative atomic mass
blocks.text: The relative atomic mass, Ar, of an element is the average mass of its isotopes: Ar = sum of (isotopic mass x percentage abundance) / 100. The abundances are given or read from the mass spectrum.

blocks.alt: Top: the mass spectrum of boron, bars at m/e 10 (19.9%) and 11 (80.1%), with Ar = (19.9 x 10 + 80.1 x 11)/100 = 10.80. Below, four stick patterns: one Cl, peaks at 35 and 37 in the ratio 3:1; two Cl, peaks at 70, 72 and 74 in 9:6:1; one Br, peaks at 79 and 81 in 1:1; two Br, peaks at 158, 160 and 162 in 1:2:1.
blocks.caption: Isotope peaks of boron, chlorine and bromine (original stick spectra after the book's mass spectra).
blocks.long_description: Each isotope gives its own peak, and the peak heights follow the natural abundances. Chlorine (35 and 37 in 3:1) and bromine (79 and 81 in about 1:1) therefore give their compounds characteristic groups of peaks two mass units apart.

blocks.prompt: Gallium is 60.1% 69Ga and 39.9% 71Ga. Calculate its relative atomic mass.

items: Ar = sum (mass x % abundance) / 100: O 16.00, B 10.80, Cl 35.5.
